zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, supplied page subset, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); [dataset documentation](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The transcription and physical lineation are based on the supplied BnF scan, not copied from the lexical index.

runs.text: Couſas que ſe prohibem ao do-

lines.note: Qincǒmot is explained through things forbidden to a sick person and things permitted to that person. The scan restores the initial Q, prohibem, and the physical do- division; the preceding page's catchword points to this entry.

runs.text: ente nociuas, & outras boas que ſe lhe con-

lines.note: This completes doente and contrasts harmful forbidden things with beneficial ones that are allowed. The ending con- belongs to concedem on the following physical line.
The short continuation completes concedem, finishing the contrast between prohibited and permitted things in the patient's regimen. It is an actual separate printed line, not a detached headword.
Sugi and fone correspond to sinews and bones, matching Neruos and oßos. The final Portuguese noun has the double-s ligature, not the draft's oſtos, and the Japanese checked final t is retained.
This Qincu denotes an excellent maxim or saying. It is a distinct entry from the identically spelled headword below, whose gloss concerns offensive remarks.
The second Qincu is specified by Imaximuru cu and begins the explanation of an utterance that causes offence. The initial is an ordinary roman Q, not a detached italic O.

runs.text: deſatẽtadamente, ou de propoſito com que ſe

lines.note: Such a remark may be made heedlessly or deliberately. The nasal abbreviation in deſatẽtadamente remains on e; the sentence continues into the effect on its hearer below.

runs.text: da no coração dalguem, como ſe quando hum

lines.note: The phrase da no coração says that the remark strikes or wounds someone's feelings, rather than using a noun dano. The small separation after da is retained, and the sentence begins an illustrative comparison.

runs.text: falaße dos cegos mal diante dalgum delles.

lines.note: The illustration is speaking ill of blind people in the presence of one of them, explaining why the utterance is hurtful. Retain falaße, dalgum and delles as printed historical forms.
Qincuuo yǔ is the verbal expression for uttering such remarks. The Japanese example is roman; the Portuguese divides palauras after pa- at the edge.
The continuation completes palauras and specifies remarks that touch another person personally. The nasal spelling tocão belongs to the source and is not normalized.
Qindachi is glossed as the son of a noble Cugue, identifying a court-aristocratic child. Cugue occurs within the Portuguese definition and is not a Japanese example or separate headword.

The Japanese paraphrase Chicaqi yo is a near or recent age, matching the Portuguese reference to an age only recently past. Damage in ca obscured the word in the draft, but the scan supports Chicaqi and a space before yo.

This completes the relative clause: the age has recently passed. The worn vowel before final u is read as o in paßou from its rounded surviving outline and the sentence's meaning. The damage prevents complete certainty against the draft's e, so this chosen reading remains a nonblocking caveat.
Qindan means a prohibition or strict law. The ordinary roman initial Q and the full word Prohibição are restored; Co- begins the example continued on the next row.

The example says that killing living things is prohibited in this lake, with the Portuguese below specifying fishing. Preserve mizzuvmiua, xexxǒ, the caron and the split goza- rather than replacing the historical forms.

runs.text: Prohibeſe riguroſamente que não ſe peſ-

lines.note: The final ru completes gozaru. The Portuguese renders the rule as a strict prohibition on fishing; riguroſamente is legible despite damage, and peſ- continues on the next row.
This completes peſque and locates the fishing prohibition in this lake. The short line closes the preceding example, and the locally aligned spelling neste is retained.
Coganeno iye, literally houses of gold, is glossed as gilded houses. The definition continues with an alternative on the single printed line below.

The alternative is palaces, completing the Qinden entry. There is only one such printed continuation: the draft's additional c1-l021 is a duplicate recognition of this row and is removed rather than transcribed as another line.
The compound denotes rich palaces, matching the Portuguese gloss. The tightly joined Paçosricos is retained as in the aligned draft; the final u in xicacu is visible.
Qine denotes a pestle for pounding rice. The scan shows an ordinary roman Q, and Vt introduces the instrumental expression Qinede continued below.
The example means to pound rice with a pestle. The final Portuguese pilão, with its tilde on a, is restored from the scan in place of the garbled draft reading.
Qiqinno toxi paraphrases Qinen as a famine year. The headword begins with a normal Q without the draft's spurious internal separation; the doubled n of Anno is retained.

runs.text: Deprecaçoẽs, ou oração que ſe faz cõ

lines.note: This second Qinen concerns supplications or prayer, not a famine year. The scan restores Deprecaçoẽs and the final nasal abbreviation cõ, with the tilde placement preserved rather than modernized.
The prayer is made with devotion and attention. The historical spelling deuação is retained; it completes the definition rather than supplying a new entry.
Qingacocu denotes neighbouring or bordering kingdoms. The meaningful consonant in confins is f, not the draft's long ſ, and the headword is one uninterrupted roman word.
The Japanese paraphrase means to apply oneself to learning. The Portuguese is Estudar split after Estu-, so the damaged vowel is u rather than the draft's i.
This completes Estudar and then gives the separate roman S. register label. The short printed continuation is retained as its own physical line.
Coganeno cotoba, words of gold, is glossed as a good saying or maxim. The headword begins with an ordinary roman Q, not the draft's detached italic O.

The gloss concludes with maxim, followed by alternatives meaning to utter such sayings. Preserve the printed comma after yǔ and the roman alternative marker l, rather than silently replacing punctuation.
This translates both Japanese verbal alternatives above as saying good maxims. The line closes the Qinguen entry and is separate from the following metals entry.
Qin guin is glossed through Cogane and xirocane as gold and silver. The scan has a space between Qin and guin but no comma there; the draft's separation after the initial Q is not a word boundary.
The single-word continuation supplies silver, completing the pair ouro and prata. It remains a physical body line despite its brevity.
The compound lists gold, silver and precious stones. The scan supports final n in Qinguin and initial x in xuguiocu, correcting the draft's m and z; ta- continues as tama below.
The initial ma completes tama, the third Japanese item. The Portuguese confirms the three-part list: gold, silver and precious stones.
Qinguiocu pairs gold with precious stones, unlike the preceding three-item compound. The initial Q is roman and belongs to the headword; pe- is the printed split of pedras.
This completes pedras precioſas and the definition of Qinguiocu. The continuation does not repeat the silver component of the preceding entry.

The gloss identifies only an herb of this name, without a species description. Enlargement shows a long ſ rather than f before caron ǒ; the supplied lexical index's Qinguisǒ supports the s reading but does not replace the printed long-s form.
Qinguiǔxi is a calf made of gold, with a caron over u in the headword. The final Palaura introduces a note about the expression's textual setting below.
The expression is identified as a word from the books of the Church, fitting the preceding golden-calf gloss. This is a usage note completing the entry, not an independent definition.

The four Japanese terms introduce four accomplishments. The first is playing musical instruments; the scan reads inſtrumen-, without the draft's extra i after t, and preserves the four comma-separated terms.

runs.text: tos, jugar certo jogo de pedrinhas, ou enxadres,

lines.note: This completes instrumentos and describes the board-game accomplishment through a game of little stones or chess. Retain the historical jugar and enxadres rather than replacing them with modern spellings.
Writing and painting complete the four-part list, corresponding to xo and gua. Both verbs belong to the same Portuguese explanation and remain on this short physical line.

runs.text: Lugar, ou pouoação perto, ou vezinha.

lines.note: Qingǒ denotes a nearby place or settlement. The scan supports caron ǒ and the historical spelling pouoação; it is distinct from the imprisonment entry below.
Qingocu is imprisonment or a prison. The example begins with the same word divided at Qingo- across the physical line boundary.

The example concerns being sentenced to imprisonment and banishment. Its Portuguese translation begins here and continues at the top of column 2, so the column boundary must not be mistaken for a new entry.

This finishes the translation begun at the foot of column 1: condemned to imprisonment and banishment. A new example then begins, with Fitouo indicating the person imprisoned and qingo- continuing below.

runs.text: Prender alguẽ, ou metelo no trõco.

lines.note: The example means to imprison someone or put them in the stocks. Retain the nasal abbreviations alguẽ and trõco; the right-edge mark is a full stop, not a continuation hyphen.
This different Qingocu denotes neighbouring or bordering kingdoms, not imprisonment. The scan supports confins and the historical comarcãos with its tilde on a.

The Japanese gloss gives returning and entering, with the Portuguese specifying re-entry into the capital on the next line. Preserve the printed nh sequence and caron ǔ rather than rewriting the romanization.
Miyaco is the place into which one returns in the preceding sentence. It is an embedded Japanese place term in Portuguese prose, not a standalone headword.
Tattoqi fito is an esteemed person, matching an honourable man in Portuguese. The scan restores fito and honrado from the draft's damaged readings, and the definition continues below.
Noble completes the description of the esteemed person. This short continuation belongs to the first Qinin entry, not the hungry-person entry that follows.
Vyeta fito describes a hungry person, and the Portuguese gives famished or dying of hunger. This is a distinct homographic Qinin entry and must not be merged with the noble-person definition.
The noun fome completes morto de fome, the description of the famished person. Its initial is f, not the draft's long ſ, a meaningful correction supported by both the glyph and the phrase.

Qinjei is a prohibition; the example means to disobey it. The scan restores Vt and Qinjeiuo. The vowel after long ſ is worn, but the chosen ſomu- best matches its rounded outline and the verb meaning, rather than the draft's ſemu-.
The initial qu completes ſomuqu, and the Portuguese says to violate the prohibition or law. Keep the physical split and the historical Quebrantar rather than modernizing the verb.
Coganeno ji specifies gold lettering. The headword's medial consonant is n, not the draft's m, and the final S. is a separate roman label.
The next Qinji is the act of forbidding, distinct from gold lettering above. Restore the ordinary roman Q; Imaximuru coto is the Japanese paraphrase, while S. remains a roman register label.
The verb's principal forms introduce forbidding or hindering. The Portuguese reads empedir, with a visible d rather than the draft's b; the historical initial e is not modernized.

The example begins with a proclamation issuing from Camacuradono. The scan supports furejǒ, not ſurejǒ, and a word space after yori. No terminal hyphen is visible after ya, although the word continues below.

This completes yamabuxiuo and says that the mountain ascetics are strictly prohibited; the translation specifies their passage. Tog. is the roman source label, and De- begins the Portuguese translation on the following row.

runs.text: cendo prouiſão de Camacuradono, em que por

lines.note: The opening cendo completes Decendo from the preceding row: an order comes down from Camacuradono. The name's damaged do is restored, and the scan's continuation indentation is reinstated.

runs.text: todas as partes manda prohibir a paßagem de

lines.note: The order commands that passage be prohibited everywhere. The scan restores the full word prohibir, and paßagem retains its double-s ligature.

Yamabuxis are the people whose passage is prohibited, completing the Portuguese sentence. The word belongs in that italic explanation as a whole; the separate S. is roman, rather than part of the mixed formatting in the draft.

This separate verbal entry means doing something carefully or exactly while excluding what is harmful. The scan restores Qinji, the nasal abbreviation algũa and exacta-, whose ct ligature is not the draft's garbled gasta.

runs.text: mente apartando, ou prohibindo todo o ruim, ou

lines.note: This completes exactamente and explains the exclusion of everything bad or unsuitable. The word is prohibindo, with a visible o rather than the draft's c.

The gloss adds anything that could hinder or harm, then begins the medicine-preparation example. Enlargement supports the wholly roman Japanese cuſurino, despite worn central letters; it is not partly Portuguese italic text.
The Japanese asks that the medicinal water be decocted with care. The form is qinjite without the draft's extra i, and yô has a circumflex; the Portuguese divides aquella after aquel-.

runs.text: la agoa da mezinha alimpandoa muito bem, &

lines.note: This completes aquella and specifies the water of the medicine, to be cleaned very thoroughly. The historical agoa, mezinha and alimpandoa are preserved rather than modernized.
The instruction ends by urging particular care in the preparation. The printed separation in eſmerando vos is preserved, and the line completes the medicine example.
Chicaqi fi refers to days near the present, and the Portuguese first gives a few days from now. The headword's final checked t is retained without expansion.
The alternative is a few days ago, showing that this entry includes recent past as well as near future. Preserve the unaccented historical ha.
Qinjo is a nearby place, exactly matching Chicaqi tocoro. The headword is a single roman word, not the draft's separated Q and injo.
Qinjǔ denotes birds and beasts, paraphrased by Tori and qedamono. The scan restores final caron ǔ, both Japanese nouns, and the printed a- division of animaes.
This completes animaes and the birds-and-beasts definition. Only one such row is printed; c2-l031 is a second OCR recognition of the same line and is removed without loss of source text.

This separate Qinju concerns attendants serving close to a lord, as explained below. The unmarked final u distinguishes the printed form from Qinjǔ above; the Portuguese ends in ſeruem, without the draft's spurious hyphen.
The attendants serve close to the lord. The example alternatives then begin with Qinjuno fito and the divided qin-, both describing members of that close service.

runs.text: Homẽs que ſeruem de perto, ou

lines.note: The initial juno completes qinjuno, and xu supplies the alternative collective expression. The Portuguese describes men serving nearby, with the abbreviation Homẽs retained.

runs.text: andão ſempre ao lado do ſenhor.

lines.note: The explanation adds that these men are always at the lord's side. Retain the printed nasal ending in andão and the long ſ in ſempre and ſenhor.

runs.text: Qin, jǔ, chǔ, guio. Tori, qedamono, mu-

lines.note: This four-part sequence lists birds, beasts, small creatures and fish, with corresponding Japanese paraphrases. Preserve both u-carons and the physical mu- division before xi.
The initial xi completes muxi, followed by vuo for fish. The Portuguese confirms all four categories; its final noun is peixes, with x rather than the draft's n.
Qinmiacu denotes the pulse. The scan has an uppercase initial Q and the Portuguese vowel u in Pulſo, correcting both the draft's separated lowercase q and Palſo.
Qinmit is something hard, strong or rigorous. Enlargement reveals the faint descending j in rija, restoring the missing consonant rather than retaining the draft's ria.
The example concerns receiving a strict order from a lord. The scan supports Qinmitni with t rather than the draft's second m, and the circumflex in vôxe; Man- begins the Portuguese verb below.

runs.text: dar o ſenhor algũa couſa teſa, & riguro-

lines.note: The initial dar completes Mandar: the lord gives an order firmly and rigorously. Preserve algũa and the physical riguro- split in the Portuguese translation.
This completes riguroſamente and closes the strict-order example. It is a genuine short continuation, not part of the next headword.
Dairino mon paraphrases the gate of the imperial palace. The headword's damaged consonant is n, not the draft's u, and pa- begins the divided Portuguese paços.
This completes the palace-gate explanation. Dairi occurs inside the Portuguese sentence and is eligible for whole-word typeface review, unlike the preceding Japanese paraphrase.
This separate Qinmon is an excellent authoritative saying or citation. The duplicated headword is intentional because its meaning differs from the preceding palace gate.
Maxim completes the alternatives in the authoritative-saying definition. Retain its long ſ and its independent physical line.
Qinmot concerns things prohibited, with Imaximuru mono as its Japanese paraphrase. The scan restores the headword and the full que in the Portuguese clause, which continues below.

The final line specifies things that a sick person is forbidden to eat. The scan restores prohibem and ao doente from the garbled draft; this closes the entry before the separate bottom-right catchword.
